column2: Struck by ignorance in childhood, by women in youth, and tormented by anxiety for his wife in the rest, what does the lowest of men do?
Non-being stands at the head of being, unloveliness at the head of the lovely, sorrows at the head of pleasures; in which one shall I take refuge?
Those persons whose opening and closing of the eyelids is the world's dissolution and arising — such persons pass away; what is the counting of ones like me?
The world itself is said to be the limit of sorrows; how can happiness be gained in the body fallen in its midst?
I am awakened, I am awakened! This is the wicked thief of the Self; I shall kill it, the mind; by the mind I have long been robbed.
Do not grieve over what is to be abandoned; do not be intent on what is to be taken; abandoning the views of abandoning and taking, abide in the remainder and be steady.
Hopelessness, fearlessness, constancy, evenness, knowledge, desirelessness, actionlessness, gentleness, freedom from conceptions;
firmness, friendliness, contentment of mind, softness, soft speech — these abide without impression in the knower freed from abandoning and taking.
The net of impressions, spread by the huntress craving who has seized, extended by the threads of anxiety, flowing in the water of the world:
cut this, dear one, with this sharp needle of intellect; having cut the net as wind a cloud, stand in the extended state.
Cutting the mind with the mind alone, like a tree with an axe, reach the purifying state and be steady at once.
Standing, going, sleeping, waking, dwelling, rising, falling — having ascertained to the end "this is unreal," abandon it.
If you take refuge in this seen, you are a conscious being, bound; if you abandon this seen, then you are mindless, liberated.
Meditating "I am not, this is not," stay immovable, within the Self and the world, in the interval between seer and seen.
Ever contemplate your own Self called seeing; free of taster and tasted, in the middle of taster and tasted,
meditating on mere tasting, become of the Supreme Self; relying on the unsupported, in the midst be steady.
Those bound by rope are freed; those bound by craving are not freed by anyone; therefore, Nidagha, abandon craving by giving up intention.
Cutting this impure one made of I-sense with the needle of non-I-sense, born of nature, in the ground of becoming, become one whose fear of all beings is quieted.
I belong to these things and they are my life; I am nothing without them, nor are they without me —
abandoning such inner conviction, reflecting with the mind: "I am not of a thing; no thing is mine."
For one doing action playfully with an inwardly cool mind, that abandonment of impressions, O Brahmin, is declared to be the aim.
He who, having made all things equal by intellect and destroyed impressions, leaves the body without possessiveness — his destruction of impressions is the one to be known.
He who has playfully given up impressions made of egoism and stays as a renouncer of objects of meditation is called liberated while living.
He who, having abandoned imagining and impressions without root, has attained peace — know this renunciation to be known: he is liberated, best of Brahmins.

These two have attained Brahman-hood, these two are free of fever; unwearied in pleasures and pains that arrive at their time; know these, renouncer and yogi, self-controlled and peaceful, O lord of sages.
For whom there are no desired or undesired things in the views within, who acts as in deep sleep — he is called liberated while living.
Who does not rejoice or sink through views of joy, anger, fear, wrath, desire or meanness, free of reflection;
craving born of impressions of outer objects is called bound; craving freed from impressions of all objects is called free.
Let this be mine — know that desire, accompanied by prayer, to be a sharp chain giving sorrow, birth and fear.
The great-minded one, always abandoning this in all states, existent and non-existent, reaches the supremely noble state.
Abandoning reliance on bondage and on liberation, even on the state of pleasure and pain, and reliance on being and non-being, stay like an unagitated great ocean.
O good man, a fourfold conviction arises in a person.
I am from foot to head made by mother and father — this is the first conviction, O Brahmin, seen from the toil of bondage.
I am beyond all states, subtler than a hair's tip — this is the second conviction that arises in the good for liberation.
I am the net of the world, the whole of the Self of things, imperishable — the third conviction is said, best of Brahmins, for liberation alone.
I, or the whole world, is void, always like space — this fourth conviction too gives the accomplishment of liberation.
Of these, the first is said to be by craving fit for bondage; the three of pure craving are clear: the liberated-while-living, the sporting ones.
The conviction "all indeed is I alone," O great-minded — taking it, the mind no more arises toward despair.
It is called the void, nature, illusion, knowledge of Brahman; Shiva, Person, Lord, and the eternal Self.
By the dual and non-dual, in the sport of making the world, the power made of the Supreme Self expands as non-dual alone.
Relying on the state beyond all, fully one, made of consciousness, neither agitated nor self-satisfied, he does not sink in the world.
Always doing the work that comes, seeing foe and friend alike, free of wished and unwished, he neither grieves nor longs.
Speaking what is pleasing to all, urged, of gentle speech, knowing the minds of beings, he does not sink in the world.
Relying on the earlier view, delighting in the abandonment of objects of meditation, be at ease in the state of liberated-while-living, move in the world free of fever.
With all hope abandoned within, passionless, free of impressions, conforming to everything outwardly, move in the world free of fever.
Outwardly with feigned activity, in the heart free of agitation, a doer outside, a non-doer within, move in the world with pure mind.
With egoism abandoned, mind comforted, shining like the sky, taking no stain or mark, move in the world with pure mind.
Noble, of gracious conduct, following all customs, within a renouncer of attachment, outwardly as if with many possessions; taking inner dispassion, outwardly acting as if intent on hope.
This is a kinsman, this is not — such counting is for the small-minded; for those of noble conduct, the whole earth is a family.
Take refuge in the state free of being and non-being, free of old age and death, free of the beginnings of quieted imagining, without passion.
This is the Brahmic state, clear, desireless, free of disease; moving about with it thus, one is not bewildered in difficulties.
By dispassion, by scripture, and by qualities such as greatness, whatever is for the removal of intention, the mind should itself raise up.
By dispassion the mind goes to fullness, subject to its destruction; by hope it becomes colored, like a clear lake in autumn.
Doing the same flavorless flood of activities again and again day after day, O wise one, why are you not ashamed?
Bondage is held by consciousness and the perceived; in its release, liberation is declared. Consciousness is not perceived — such is the Self: the summary of all doctrines.
Taking this conviction, behold with kindled intellect; you yourself, by yourself, will reach the state of bliss.
I am consciousness; these worlds are consciousness; the directions are consciousness; these creatures are consciousness. Freed from seen and seeing, of the form of the alone and spotless,
ever risen, without appearance, the seer, the witness, of the nature of consciousness.
The form of consciousness freed from the perceived, of the nature of full light, with all knowables quieted — I am the great mere awareness.
With all intentions quieted, all desires stilled, having reached the state free of conceptions, be at ease in yourself, O lord of sages.

Thus. The Brahmin who daily studies this Mahopanishad, though not a scholar becomes a scholar; though uninitiated becomes initiated; he becomes purified by fire; purified by wind; purified by soma; purified by truth; purified by all.

He becomes known to all gods; he becomes bathed in all holy places; he becomes contemplated by all gods; he becomes one who has performed all sacrifices. The fruits of sixty thousand recitations of the Gayatri are obtained; the fruits of a hundred thousand recitations of histories and Puranas are obtained.

Ten thousand recitations of Om are obtained. He purifies a row of the unseeing; he purifies seven generations of men. So said the revered Hiranyagarbha. By recitation he attains immortality — thus the Upanishad.
Om. The point of light is the supreme meditation, established in the heart of the universal Self — atomic, Shambhava, peaceful, gross, subtle and supreme.
Full of difficulty, hard to worship, hard to see, free, imperishable, that meditation is rare even for sages and the wise.
Of regulated food, conquering anger, conquering attachment, conquering the senses, free of dualities, free of egoism, without hope, without possessions,
who makes the unreachable reachable, whose mind brings what is to be reached — in the mouth they find three; the swan of three abodes is so called.
Know it as the most secret, free of laziness, without support; the subtle digit of the form of soma is that supreme state of Vishnu.
Three-faced, threefold in quality, the abode, of three elements, devoid of form, motionless, free of conceptions, formless, without support.
The abode free of limiting adjuncts, beyond speech and mind, nature itself, to be grasped by being, uncompounded, fallen from no station.
Beyond manifold bliss, hard to see, liberation, imperishable; to be contemplated as thus freed, eternal, firm, undying.
That is of Brahman, that is the inner Self, that is of Vishnu, that is the supreme refuge; inconceivable, the Self of consciousness, the supreme space that stands.
Not empty, yet of the nature of void, beyond void, established in the heart; neither meditation nor meditator nor object of meditation, yet itself the object of meditation.
Neither all, nor void, nor the supreme, nor higher than the highest; inconceivable, unawakened; they know it as neither true nor supreme.
It is engaged by sages; neither gods nor others know the supreme. Greed, delusion, fear, pride, desire, anger, and sin,
cold and heat, hunger and thirst, intention and doubt, pride of Brahmin birth, and the heap of knots of liberation — none of these are there;
neither fear nor pleasure nor pain, nor honor and dishonor; free of such states, that is the Brahman to be grasped, the supreme.
Yama, Niyama, renunciation, silence, place and time, posture, Mulabandha, equality of the body, and fixing the gaze,
control of breath, withdrawal, concentration, meditation on the Self, and samadhi — the limbs are declared in order.
By the knowledge "all is Brahman," the restraint of the group of senses is declared to be Yama; it should be practiced again and again.
The flow of the same kind and rejection of the different kind — that is Niyama, supreme bliss; the wise practice it through Niyama.
Renunciation is the giving up of the world's form by beholding the Self as being-consciousness; renunciation is honored by the great and gives liberation at once.
From which speech turns back, not reaching it along with the mind, that silence which yogis attain — the wise should always practice it.
From which words turn back, who can describe that? If the world is to be spoken of, that too is free of words.
Or that is silence, called all-natural; the silence of speech is for children and is not fitting for knowers of Brahman.
In the beginning, end and middle, where people do not exist, which is constantly pervaded by this — that place is called solitary.
The imagination of all beings, of Brahma and others, in a twinkling, is indicated by the word "time"; indeed it is undivided bliss, non-dual.
That in which continuous contemplation of Brahman goes on with ease — know that as posture; another destroys ease.
For accomplishment, the foundation of the universe, the origin of all beings, the non-dual — in which the perfected have attained perfection, that is called the perfect posture.
The root of all worlds, the root of the binding of mind — the Mulabandha is always to be practiced; it is fit for knowers of Brahman.
Know the equality of limbs: it dissolves in the equal Brahman; otherwise there is no true equality, only stiffness like a dry tree.
Making the vision full of knowledge, one should see the world as Brahman; that vision is supremely noble, not the one fixed on the tip of the nose.
Where the cessation of seer, seeing and seen occurs, there the gaze should be set, not on the tip of the nose.
By contemplating Brahman-ness in all states such as the mind, the restraint of all modifications is called pranayama.
The negation of the world is called exhalation; the modification "I am Brahman" is called inhalation.
Then the steadiness of that modification is retention, the control of breath; this too is, for the awakened, only a pinching of the nose of the ignorant.
Seeing the Self in objects, the coloring of the mind's thought, is to be known as pratyahara; it should be practiced again and again.
Wherever the mind goes, by seeing Brahman there, holding the mind is concentration; that is held to be the highest concentration.
Abiding in the modification "I am Brahman" without support is known by the word meditation, and gives supreme bliss.
By the modification of changelessness, by taking the form of Brahman again, the complete forgetting of modifications is called samadhi.
